subsections.subsection_title: Obesity in Breast Cancer Diagnosis and Treatment
subsections.content:
In 2020, breast cancer was the most common cancer and the leading cause of cancer death in women globally, with 2.3 million incident cases and 0.7 million deaths estimated. As of the end of 2020, there were 7.8 million women worldwide who had survived at least 5 years after a breast cancer diagnosis. Higher body fatness and adult weight gain have been established as risk factors for postmenopausal breast cancer, in particular hormone-sensitive breast cancers. With the increasing global prevalence of overweight and obesity, it is expected that many women diagnosed with breast cancer will have excess body weight, but the impact on breast cancer outcomes has been less clear than for incidence.

Previous meta-analyses of epidemiologic studies published up to 30 June, 2012 included in the World Cancer Research Fund/American Institute for Cancer Research (WCRF/AICR) Third Export Report showed increased risks of all-cause mortality and breast cancer-specific mortality with higher postdiagnosis BMI. In addition, women of normal body weight (BMI of 18.5-24.9 kg/m 2 ) after a breast cancer diagnosis were shown to have a more favorable overall survival than women of other weight statuses. Despite these statistically significant associations, the evidence was judged as limited-suggestive because of limitations in the design or conduct of the observational studies. In particular, the potential for residual confounding and reverse causation limited the confidence to determine causality. Women with obesity may have more treatment complications and may receive less effective treatment compared with women without obesity ref [4]. Furthermore, cancer treatments may alter body weight and composition and could lead to adverse metabolic consequences ref [5]. Not all studies included in the meta-analyses reported information on breast cancer subtypes;

although the association appeared to be similar in women with hormone receptor-positive or -negative breast cancers ref [4], the relationship was less clear in women with aggressive tumors, such as triplenegative breast cancers ref [4]. Breast cancer patients can have a long survival time and remain at risk of recurrence long after diagnosis. Therefore, understanding the impact of postdiagnosis body fatness on breast cancer outcomes is important for identifying potentially actionable lifestyle targets for the growing number of women living with and beyond breast cancer ref [4]. We conducted updated systematic literature reviews and meta-analyses to summarize the evidence published until and after 30 June 2012 of the previous report

subsections.subsection_title: Secondary Outcomes, Weight Intervention, and Surgical Context
subsections.content:
In the case of multiple publications from the same or overlapping populations, the publication with the largest number of events was selected for inclusion in the meta-analysis. Study and participants' characteristics and results were extracted into the CUP Global database. Study selection and data extraction was checked by a second reviewer. Any disagreements were resolved by consensus. The quality of individual studies was not graded using a specific tool. Instead, relevant study characteristics that could be used to explore potential sources of bias were included into the CUP Global database. For all the included studies, information on potential for selection bias, information bias of exposure and outcome assessment, and residual confounding by cancer stage and treatment was retrieved after identifying the most likely influential sources of bias in cancer survival studies. The potential influence of measurement error, length of follow-up and loss to follow-up, and adjustment for confounding factors on results was tested in subgroup meta-analyses and meta-regression analyses. Details on how the study authors addressed the potential biases were also included. In the Expert Panel meeting, whether the studies had serious quality issues were discussed when judging the evidence for each exposure-outcome association.

The summary relative risk (RR) estimates and their 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using the inverse variance randomeffects model. When at least three (additional) studies were identified in the updated search, a linear dose-response meta-analysis was conducted (or updated if reviewed previously with evidence up to 30 June, 2012) if the studies reported sufficient information for analysis, otherwise the studies were descriptively synthesized. The multivariable adjusted RR estimates per exposure increment unit were pooled in a dose-response meta-analysis either with estimates provided in the original publications or estimated by us using the generalized weighted least-squares regression model. Standard imputations were conducted to calculate the required information when missing (0-57% across analyses) (Text S1).

In the linear dose-response meta-analysis, the underweight group (BMI <18.5 kg/m 2 or as defined by studies) was excluded to avoid possible impact on the risk estimation. Pre-to postdiagnosis (≥1 year) weight change was grouped into moderate (5-10%), or high (>10%) weight loss or gain. The RR estimates for the weight change vs stable weight (±5% or as defined by studies) groups were pooled in categorical meta-analyses, informed by studies of weight change and prognosis in breast cancer survivors ref [34].

Between-study heterogeneity was assessed by the Cochran's Q test and I 2 statistic, accompanied by visual inspection of the forest plots for consistency of associations, which contributes towards evidence grading. Pre-defined subgroup meta-analyses and randomeffects meta-regression analyses were conducted to explore if a certain disease or study characteristics or aspect of risk of bias explain between-study heterogeneity. This included the exploration of the potential influence of changes in treatment regimens, over time, on the associations, by grouping the studies according to the diagnosis or treatment period: before 2000 or after 2000 for the shift to include doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide in chemotherapy, and before 2005 or after 2005 for the reduced anthracycline use and the introduction of taxanes, and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) targeted therapy-trastuzumab. Small study effects such as publication bias was examined using Egger's test and visual inspection of the funnel plots for asymmetry, when there were more than 10 studies. Individual studies may potentially influence the summary RR estimate and was examined by leave-one-out analysis. Restricted cubic spline regression with three knots at 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles of distribution of the exposure was conducted and pooled in random-effects meta-analysis when five or more studies, each with data for at least three exposure categories, including the underweight group if presented, were available. The linear and nonlinear models were compared using a likelihood ratio test. A two-tailed P value of <.1 was considered as evidence for small study effects or between-study heterogeneity in the generally lowpowered Egger's test and meta-regression analyses.

An independent Expert Panel (ELG, MJG, AAJ, EK, VL, SKC and AMT) graded the quality of the evidence into strong (subgrades evaluating likelihood of causality: convincing, probable, or substantial effect on risk unlikely) or limited (subgrades evaluating likelihood of causality: limited-suggestive or limited-no conclusion) level, using pre-defined evidence grading criteria. One RCT was identified ref [36]. All others were observational studies, including studies on second primary tumours ref [33], endocrine therapy-related endometrial cancer outcomes ref [32], weight change during chemotherapy and prognosis ref [34], and surgical and oncological outcomes in breast-conserving surgery contexts ref [35]. The publications included or excluded in each specific meta-analysis or descriptive synthesis and the reasons for exclusion, and the corresponding study description and participants' characteristics are provided in Tables S3 and S4-S8. Below is an overview of the findings. Table 1 shows the summary findings and the judgment of the Expert Panel.

subsections.subsection_title: Prognostic impact of adiposity in early breast cancer
subsections.content: The epidemiologic evidence on body fatness, weight change and breast cancer prognosis was systematically synthesized and independently evaluated, drawing on prior systematic review and meta-analytic evidence as well as multiple clinical trial and pooled cohort analyses ref [53], ref [15], ref [52], ref [51], ref [50], ref [42], ref [56], ref [57], ref [55], ref [49], ref [47], ref [54], ref [48]. The estimated increase in risk per 5 kg/m 2 higher postdiagnosis BMI was 7% for all-cause mortality, 10% for breast cancer-specific mortality and 14% for second primary breast cancer ref [53], ref [42], ref [50], ref [51]. There was high, partially explained, between-study heterogeneity, but the positive associations were generally consistent across several study and disease subgroups ref [53], ref [15], ref [52], ref [56], ref [57], ref [55], ref [49], ref [47], ref [54]. However, most subgroups included a low number of studies and will require further analyses in the future ref [53], ref [50], ref [42].

subsections.subsection_title: Treatment-specific implications across endocrine, HER2-directed, and metastatic settings
subsections.content:
The epidemiologic evidence on body fatness, weight change and breast cancer prognosis was systematically synthesized and independently evaluated. The estimated increase in risk per 5 kg/m 2 higher postdiagnosis BMI was 7% for all-cause mortality, 10% for breast cancer-specific mortality and 14% for second primary breast cancer. There was high, partially explained, between-study heterogeneity, but the positive associations were generally consistent across several study and disease subgroups, including endocrine-treated early breast cancer cohorts and metastatic settings ref [29], ref [61], ref [62], ref [63], ref [64], ref [65]. However, most subgroups included a low number of studies and will require further analyses in the future.

Plausible biological mechanisms underpinning the observed associations of increased body fatness with poorer survival have been widely studied. Increased conversion of androgens to oestrogens by aromatase in adipose fat, decreased levels of sex-hormone binding globulin and the resulting increased circulating oestrogen levels may drive breast cancer progression in postmenopausal women with obesity, which is particularly relevant when interpreting findings from endocrine therapy trials ref [29], ref [61], ref [62], ref [64], ref [65]. Other potential mediators include insulin resistance and associated increased insulin levels; chronic sub-clinical inflammation; and altered adipokine levels. These inter-connected signaling pathways could promote tumor growth and proliferation in women with obesity. In the present review, there was evidence that the association with breast cancer recurrence were, on average, inverse among women with metastatic disease but positive among women with early-stage diseases, a pattern broadly compatible with reports in advanced and HER2-positive disease settings ref [58], ref [59], ref [60], ref [63]. The results may reflect disease characteristics (tumor biology and treatment responses) rather than host factors (obesity and its metabolic consequences) may have greater impact on recurrence and survival in these distinctive survivors. Further studies are needed to elucidate such findings.

The present nonlinear analysis of postdiagnosis BMI and all-cause mortality revealed a J-shaped relationship suggesting a more favorable survival in women of high normal to low overweight (24-26 kg/m 2 ) compared with women of low normal weight (arbitrary chosen at 20 kg/m 2 ). This observation relates somewhat to the phenomenon of the "obesity paradox" that has been reported in other cancer patients and in pooled HER2-positive breast cancer trial data ref [58]. The exact causes are unclear but could include metabolic advantage, collider stratification bias (selection bias), confounding and/or reverse causation bias. In addition, BMI does not reflect fat distribution and cannot distinguish lean from fat mass. Analyses conducted for waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio in the present review showed positive associations with all-cause and breast cancerspecific mortality, which may be independent of BMI. Sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity may also be independent prognostic factors for breast cancer, but further investigations are needed to study in more detail associations with body shape and composition. Taken together, the evidence was graded as strong (subgrade: probable) for body fatness and all-cause mortality, breast cancer-specific mortality and second primary breast cancer. The evidence for BMI and higher risk of breast cancer recurrence was graded as limited-suggestive since the outcomes were inconsistently defined across the studies, including variation across endocrine therapy and metastatic treatment trials ref [29], ref [59], ref [60], ref [62], ref [63], ref [65], and could be misclassified and/or incompletely ascertained in observational studies that used participants' reported or registry record linkage data. The evidence for BMI and higher risks of nonbreast cancer-related mortality and cardiovascular mortality was also graded as limited-suggestive. There was a paucity of data on cardiovascular mortality, despite cardiovascular deaths being the most common cause of nonbreast cancer deaths in breast cancer patients, and high BMI may increase cardiovascular events in general. More research is needed to investigate these important outcomes.

Relatively few numbers of studies investigated weight or BMI change and the results were substantially heterogeneous. Weight loss after cancer diagnosis may be associated with higher all-cause mortality, but the intentionality of weight loss was unclear and could be related to cancer cachexia. In the pooling project, the positive association with large weight loss was only restricted to the under or normal weight individuals, those with comorbidities, and who ever smoked, hence the overall results could be affected by reverse causation. In addition, we found no apparent associations between weight or BMI gain and breast cancer outcomes across the timeframes, unlike a recent published meta-analysis that reported negative prognostic impact with large weight gain overall. The association may be distorted, as chemotherapy may cause weight gain particularly in patients treated with older regimens that often incorporated high doses of corticosteroids; in metastatic chemotherapy-treated cohorts, BMI associations have also varied ref [63]. The evidence was judged as limited-no conclusion.

We only identified one small weight loss intervention trial publishing results on survival outcomes, which suggested beneficial effects of intervention through diet, physical activity and behavioral change compared with education. Treatment-specific observational evidence nevertheless suggests that the prognostic implications of adiposity may differ across tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitor, ovarian suppression, HER2-directed, and metastatic endocrine therapy settings ref [29], ref [58], ref [59], ref [60], ref [61], ref [62], ref [64], ref [65], which were expected to have better treatment protocols and management. The evidence of greater body fatness causing increased mortality was unlikely to be caused solely by chance or bias, and was graded as strong probable evidence. To reach the strong convincing grade, more definitive evidence from RCTs (body composition, weight control or weight loss trials) is needed.

The epidemiologic evidence on body fatness, weight change and breast cancer prognosis was systematically synthesized and independently evaluated. The estimated increase in risk per 5 kg/m 2 higher postdiagnosis BMI was 7% for all-cause mortality, 10% for breast cancer-specific mortality and 14% for second primary breast cancer. There was high, partially explained, between-study heterogeneity, but the positive associations were generally consistent across several study and disease subgroups. However, most subgroups included a low number of studies and will require further analyses in the future.

Increased conversion of androgens to oestrogens by aromatase in adipose fat, decreased levels of sex-hormone binding globulin and the resulting increased circulating oestrogen levels may drive breast cancer progression in postmenopausal women with obesity. Other potential mediators include insulin resistance and associated increased insulin levels; chronic sub-clinical inflammation; and altered adipokine levels, including increased leptin that is proinflammatory and decreased adiponectin and the consequent reduced anti-inflammatory and insulin-sensitising effects. These inter-connected signaling pathways could promote tumor growth and proliferation in women with obesity. In the present review, there was evidence that the association with breast cancer recurrence were, on average, inverse among women with metastatic disease but positive among women with early-stage diseases. The results may reflect disease characteristics (tumor biology and treatment responses) rather than host factors (obesity and its metabolic consequences) may have greater impact on recurrence and survival in these distinctive survivors. Further studies are needed to elucidate such findings.

The present nonlinear analysis of postdiagnosis BMI and all-cause mortality revealed a J-shaped relationship suggesting a more favorable survival in women of high normal to low overweight (24-26 kg/m 2 ) compared with women of low normal weight (arbitrary chosen at 20 kg/m 2 ). This observation relates somewhat to the phenomenon of the "obesity paradox" that has been reported in other cancer patients. The exact causes are unclear but could include metabolic advantage, collider stratification bias (selection bias), confounding and/or reverse causation bias. In addition, BMI does not reflect fat distribution and cannot distinguish lean from fat mass. Analyses conducted for waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio in the present review showed positive associations with all-cause and breast cancerspecific mortality, which may be independent of BMI. Sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity may also be independent prognostic factors for breast cancer, but further investigations are needed to study in more detail associations with body shape and composition. Taken together, the evidence was graded as strong (subgrade: probable) for body fatness and all-cause mortality, breast cancer-specific mortality and second primary breast cancer. The evidence for BMI and higher risk of breast cancer recurrence was graded as limited-suggestive since the outcomes were inconsistently defined across the studies, and could be misclassified and/or incompletely ascertained in observational studies that used participants' reported or registry record linkage data. The evidence for BMI and higher risks of nonbreast cancer-related mortality and cardiovascular mortality was also graded as limited-suggestive. There was a paucity of data on cardiovascular mortality, despite cardiovascular deaths being the most common cause of nonbreast cancer deaths in breast cancer patients, and high BMI may increase cardiovascular events in general. More research is needed to investigate these important outcomes.

Relatively few numbers of studies investigated weight or BMI change and the results were substantially heterogeneous. Weight loss after cancer diagnosis may be associated with higher all-cause mortality, but the intentionality of weight loss was unclear and could be related to cancer cachexia. In addition, we found no apparent associations between weight or BMI gain and breast cancer outcomes across the timeframes, unlike a recent published meta-analysis that reported negative prognostic impact with large weight gain overall ref [67]. The association may be distorted, as chemotherapy may cause weight gain particularly in patients treated with older regimens that often incorporated high doses of corticosteroids ref [67]. The evidence was judged as limited-no conclusion.

We only identified one small weight loss intervention trial publishing results on survival outcomes, which suggested beneficial effects of intervention through diet, physical activity and behavioral change compared with education. Women with obesity receiving adjuvant or dose-dense chemotherapy may also experience higher rates of treatment-related toxicity, particularly when dosing is based on unadjusted body surface area ref [27] ref [66], which were expected to have better treatment protocols and management. The evidence of greater body fatness causing increased mortality was unlikely to be caused solely by chance or bias, and was graded as strong probable evidence. To reach the strong convincing grade, more definitive evidence from RCTs (body composition, weight control or weight loss trials) is needed.

subsections.subsection_title: Biological mechanisms linking obesity to breast cancer outcomes
subsections.content:

Other potential mediators include insulin resistance and associated increased insulin levels ref [69], ref [71]; chronic sub-clinical inflammation ref [68], ref [69], ref [70], ref [72];

and altered adipokine levels ref [69], ref [70], ref [72], including increased leptin that is proinflammatory and decreased adiponectin and the consequent reduced anti-inflammatory and insulin-sensitising effects ref [69], ref [70], ref [72]. These inter-connected signaling pathways could promote tumor growth and proliferation in women with obesity ref [68], ref [69], ref [70], ref [71], ref [72]. In the present review, there was evidence that the association with breast cancer recurrence were, on average, inverse among women with metastatic disease but positive among women with early-stage diseases. The results may reflect disease characteristics (tumor biology and treatment responses) rather than host factors (obesity and its metabolic consequences) may have greater impact on recurrence and survival in these distinctive survivors. Further studies are needed to elucidate such findings.

The present nonlinear analysis of postdiagnosis BMI and all-cause mortality revealed a J-shaped relationship suggesting a more favorable survival in women of high normal to low overweight (24-26 kg/m 2 ) compared with women of low normal weight (arbitrary chosen at 20 kg/m 2 ). This observation relates somewhat to the phenomenon of the "obesity paradox" that has been reported in other cancer patients ref [69], ref [70]. The exact causes are unclear but could include metabolic advantage, collider stratification bias (selection bias), confounding and/or reverse causation bias ref [69], ref [70]. In addition, BMI does not reflect fat distribution and cannot distinguish lean from fat mass ref [68], ref [70], ref [72]. Analyses conducted for waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio in the present review showed positive associations with all-cause and breast cancerspecific mortality, which may be independent of BMI. Sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity may also be independent prognostic factors for breast cancer ref [70], ref [72], but further investigations are needed to study in more detail associations with body shape and composition ref [68], ref [70], ref [72]. Taken together, the evidence was graded as strong (subgrade:

probable) for body fatness and all-cause mortality, breast cancer-specific mortality and second primary breast cancer. The evidence for BMI and higher risk of breast cancer recurrence was graded as limited-suggestive since the outcomes were inconsistently defined across the studies, and could be misclassified and/or incompletely ascertained in observational studies that used participants' reported or registry record linkage data. The evidence for BMI and higher risks of nonbreast cancer-related mortality and cardiovascular mortality was also graded as limited-suggestive. There was a paucity of data on cardiovascular mortality, despite cardiovascular deaths being the most common cause of nonbreast cancer deaths in breast cancer patients, and high BMI may increase cardiovascular events in general ref [68], ref [69]. More research is needed to investigate these important outcomes.

Relatively few numbers of studies investigated weight or BMI change and the results were substantially heterogeneous. Weight loss after cancer diagnosis may be associated with higher all-cause mortality, but the intentionality of weight loss was unclear and could be related to cancer cachexia. In the pooling project, the positive association with large weight loss was only restricted to the under or normal weight individuals, those with comorbidities, and who ever smoked, 52 hence the overall results could be affected by reverse causation. In addition, we found no apparent associations between weight or BMI gain and breast cancer outcomes across the timeframes, unlike a recent published meta-analysis that reported negative prognostic impact with large weight gain overall. The association may be distorted, as chemotherapy may cause weight gain particularly in patients treated with older regimens that often incorporated high doses of corticosteroids. The evidence was judged as limited-no conclusion.

We only identified one small weight loss intervention trial publishing results on survival outcomes, which suggested beneficial effects of intervention through diet, physical activity and behavioral change compared with education. 256 45,48,54,59,63,64,68,70,88,ref [102]ref [103] which were expected to have better treatment protocols and management. The evidence of greater body fatness causing increased mortality was unlikely to be caused solely by chance or bias, and was graded as strong probable evidence. To reach the strong convincing grade, more definitive evidence from RCTs (body composition, weight control or weight loss trials ref [68], ref [70]) is needed.

subsections.subsection_title: Measurement, intervention, and outcome interpretation considerations
subsections.content:
The epidemiologic evidence on body fatness, weight change and breast cancer prognosis was systematically synthesized and independently evaluated. The estimated increase in risk per 5 kg/m 2 higher postdiagnosis BMI was 7% for all-cause mortality, 10% for breast cancer-specific mortality and 14% for second primary breast cancer. There was high, partially explained, between-study heterogeneity, but the positive associations were generally consistent across several study and disease subgroups. However, most subgroups included a low number of studies and will require further analyses in the future.

Increased conversion of androgens to oestrogens by aromatase in adipose fat, decreased levels of sex-hormone binding globulin and the resulting increased circulating oestrogen levels may drive breast cancer progression in postmenopausal women with obesity. Other potential mediators include insulin resistance and associated increased insulin levels; chronic sub-clinical inflammation; and altered adipokine levels, including increased leptin that is proinflammatory and decreased adiponectin and the consequent reduced anti-inflammatory and insulin-sensitising effects. These inter-connected signaling pathways could promote tumor growth and proliferation in women with obesity. In the present review, there was evidence that the association with breast cancer recurrence were, on average, inverse among women with metastatic disease but positive among women with early-stage diseases. The results may reflect disease characteristics (tumor biology and treatment responses) rather than host factors (obesity and its metabolic consequences) may have greater impact on recurrence and survival in these distinctive survivors.
